name: Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and lactate (LBSL, DARS2)
aliases: leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and elevated lactate

clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive leukoencephalopathy caused by variants in DARS2, which encodes mitochondrial aspartyl-tRNA synthetase

The MRI pattern is highly specific: selective involvement of particular tracts rather than the whole white matter, including the cerebral white matter with sparing of the U-fibres, the pyramidal tracts and dorsal columns of the spinal cord, and defined brainstem tracts such as the medial lemniscus, superior and inferior cerebellar peduncles and the medullary pyramids
Proton MR spectroscopy typically shows raised lactate within the abnormal white matter, an important confirmatory clue

Onset ranges from infancy to adulthood; the common presentation is slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia with spasticity and dorsal-column sensory loss causing impaired proprioception and a positive Romberg sign
Deterioration or acute worsening can be provoked by minor head trauma, febrile illness or other stressors in some patients

Diagnosis rests on the combination of the selective tract pattern, elevated white-matter lactate on spectroscopy and biallelic DARS2 variants; a common intronic splice variant is frequently paired with a second allele
There is no specific treatment, so care is supportive and multidisciplinary, with physiotherapy, mobility aids and management of spasticity and sensory ataxia
reference.pathophysiology: LBSL is caused by biallelic variants in DARS2, which encodes the mitochondrial enzyme that charges transfer RNA with aspartate for mitochondrial protein synthesis. Reduced enzyme activity, often driven by a leaky intronic splice-site variant that lowers the amount of correctly spliced transcript, impairs translation of mitochondrially encoded respiratory-chain subunits in neural tissue. The resulting energy deficit and mitochondrial dysfunction selectively affect long myelinated tracts with high metabolic demand, producing the distinctive pattern of tract-specific white-matter signal change and the elevated lactate seen on spectroscopy.
additionalDifferentials: Other mitochondrial leukoencephalopathies and MELAS-spectrum disorders
Multiple sclerosis and other inflammatory demyelination
Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency (dorsal column involvement)
Hereditary spastic paraplegia with white matter change
Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem involvement from other tRNA synthetase defects
Adult-onset vanishing white matter disease and other genetic leukoencephalopathies
additionalInvestigations: Brain and spinal cord MRI to demonstrate the selective tract involvement and cord signal change
Proton MR spectroscopy to detect elevated lactate within affected white matter
DARS2 sequencing, including analysis for the common intronic splice variant and a second pathogenic allele
Nerve conduction and somatosensory evoked potentials to characterise dorsal-column and peripheral involvement
Blood and CSF lactate as supportive metabolic markers
Leukodystrophy or mitochondrial gene panel if targeted DARS2 testing is inconclusive
redFlags: Acute neurological deterioration following minor head trauma or febrile illness
Rapidly progressive weakness or bulbar dysfunction requiring reassessment
Severe sensory ataxia with recurrent falls and injury
Cognitive decline or seizures suggesting more extensive disease
reference.prognosis: The course of LBSL is variable but usually slowly progressive, with gradually worsening ataxia, spasticity and dorsal-column dysfunction; some patients remain mildly affected for many years, while early-onset cases can be more severe. Episodic decline after stressors and cumulative disability influence outcome, and life expectancy is often relatively preserved in milder phenotypes.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis by not appreciating the selective tract pattern and treating it as non-specific white matter change
Failing to perform MR spectroscopy and thereby overlooking the elevated white-matter lactate
Mislabelling the presentation as multiple sclerosis and exposing the patient to unnecessary immunotherapy
Not testing for the common intronic DARS2 variant, which can be missed by some assays
Overlooking the risk of stress- or trauma-related deterioration when counselling patients
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Supportive management as no disease-modifying therapy exists, with physiotherapy and mobility aids for progressive cerebellar ataxia and spasticity
Antispasticity treatment such as baclofen for spasticity
Balance training and falls-prevention measures for dorsal-column proprioceptive loss and a positive Romberg sign
Avoidance and prompt treatment of stressors such as head trauma and febrile illness that can provoke acute deterioration
Occupational therapy and speech and swallowing assessment as disability progresses
Neurology, clinical genetics and rehabilitation multidisciplinary care
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive DARS2 disorder, including the common intronic splice variant
